p.src: Now the faithful of Chen Family Village carried the pigs, sheep, sacrificial wine, Wukong, and Bajie in a noisy procession straight into the Temple of Divine Inspiration, where they set everything in place; they placed the boy and girl at the head of the offerings. Wukong looked back and saw incense, flowers, and candles upon the offering table. In the center stood a tablet inscribed in gold, “The God, Great King of Divine Inspiration,” but there was no other divine image. When the faithful had arranged everything, they all kowtowed before the altar and prayed, “Revered Great King, at this hour upon this day and month of this year, Chen Cheng and the other faithful of Chen Family Village, your worshippers of sundry ages, respectfully observe the annual custom by offering one boy, Chen Guanbao, one girl, Chen Yichengjin, and the prescribed number of pigs, sheep, and vessels of sacrificial wine, all presented for Your Majesty’s enjoyment. Bless us with timely winds and rains and abundant harvests of every grain.” After the prayer, they burned the paper horses and returned to their respective homes.

We must wait until that Great King comes to eat us; only then will we have carried the matter through from beginning to end. Otherwise, if he brings calamity upon them again, our work will have done more harm than good.”

p.src: The monster blocked the temple gate and asked, “Which family provides this year’s sacrifice?” Wukong answered with a smile, “Since Your Majesty asks, the village heads are the families of Chen Cheng and Chen Qing.” Hearing this answer, the monster grew suspicious and thought, “This boy is bold and quick of speech. Those brought here for me in other years never speak when I first question them. When I ask again, terror drives the soul from their bodies; by the time I reach out to seize them, they are already dead. How can today’s boy be so skilled at answering me?” The monster dared not seize him and asked again, “What are the names of the boy and girl?” Wukong replied with a smile, “The boy is Chen Guanbao, and the girl is Yichengjin.” The monster said, “This sacrifice is an ancient annual custom. Now that you have been offered to me, I ought to eat you.” Wukong replied, “I would not dare resist. Please enjoy yourself as you please.” Even after hearing this, the monster dared not lay hands on him. Blocking the gate, he shouted, “Do not answer me back! Every year I eat the boy first, but this year I shall eat the girl first instead.” Bajie panicked and said, “Your Majesty, please follow the old custom. You must not set a bad precedent.”

p.src: Without another word, the monster reached out to seize Bajie. The idiot sprang down with a thump, resumed his true form, pulled out his rake, and struck with both hands. The monster jerked back his hand and fled, while a loud clang rang out. “I broke through his armor!” said Bajie. Wukong also resumed his true form and looked: what had fallen were two fish scales, each as large as a platter of ice. He shouted, “After him!” The two of them leapt into the air. As the monster had come only to attend the feast, he had brought no weapon. Empty-handed among the clouds, he demanded, “What monks are you, and where are you from, that you come here to bully me, ruin my worship, and sully my name?” Wukong said, “So this wretch knows nothing! We are disciples of the holy monk Tripitaka of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, who travels by imperial command to the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures. Last night we lodged with the Chen family and heard of a fiend who falsely calls himself Divine Inspiration and demands a boy and girl in sacrifice every year. Out of compassion, we came to save those lives and capture you, wretch. Confess truthfully while there is still time: if you eat two children a year, for how many years have you styled yourself Great King here? How many boys and girls have you eaten? Return every one of them to me in full, and I shall spare your life.” At these words the monster fled. Bajie swung his rake at him again but missed, and the creature transformed into a violent gale and plunged into the River That Reaches Heaven.

Let us wait until tomorrow, devise a way to capture him, and take our master across the river.” Bajie agreed and went straight back into the temple, where he carried the pigs, sheep, sacrificial wine, and even the tables themselves back to the Chen house. At that time the Tang Elder, Sha the Monk, and the Chen brothers were waiting for news in the hall. Suddenly they saw Wukong and Bajie dump the pigs, sheep, and other offerings into the courtyard. The two old men were overjoyed. They immediately ordered the side rooms swept and beds prepared, then invited master and disciples to retire for the night.

p.src: Now the monster, having escaped with his life, returned beneath the waters and sat in his palace without a word. His aquatic kin, great and small, asked, “Your Majesty always returns joyfully from the annual sacrifice. Why are you troubled today?” The monster replied, “In other years, after enjoying the sacrifice, I always brought back some leftovers for all of you, but today even I did not get a single bite. My luck was poor: I met a formidable foe and nearly lost my life.” The water creatures asked, “Who was it, Your Majesty?” The monster replied, “They were disciples of a holy monk from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land who is going to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. They disguised themselves as a boy and girl and sat inside the temple. They forced me to reveal my true form, and I barely escaped with my life. I have long heard people say that Tang Tripitaka is a good man cultivated through ten incarnations and that anyone who eats a piece of his flesh will gain longevity and immortality. I never expected him to have such disciples under his command. They have ruined my reputation and destroyed my worship. I should like to capture the Tang Monk, but I fear I may not be able to do it.”

p.src: From among the water creatures there stepped forward a mottled mandarin-fish crone. Bowing repeatedly to the monster, she smiled and said, “What difficulty can there be in capturing the Tang Monk, Your Majesty? But if he is caught, might I be rewarded with some wine and meat?” The monster said, “If you have a plan, join forces with us. Once the Tang Monk is caught, I shall make you my sworn sister, and we shall feast upon him at the same table.” The mandarin-fish crone bowed her thanks and said, “I have long known that Your Majesty possesses the divine power to summon wind and rain and the might to churn the seas and overturn the rivers. But can you make snow fall?” The monster replied, “I can.” She asked again, “Since you can make snow fall, can you also bring such cold that the water freezes?” The monster said, “That too.” The mandarin-fish crone clapped her hands and laughed. “Then it is very easy indeed—very easy!” The monster said, “Then tell me how this very easy feat is to be accomplished.” The mandarin-fish crone said, “Tonight, at the third watch, Your Majesty must not hesitate. Begin your magic early: raise a blast of freezing wind and send down a heavy fall of snow, until the whole River of Heaven is frozen solid. Have those among us skilled in transformation take on human form at the crossing, some carrying packs and umbrellas, others bearing loads or pushing carts, and keep walking back and forth over the ice. The Tang Monk is desperately eager to fetch the scriptures. When he sees people crossing like this, he will certainly venture over the ice. Your Majesty can wait silently beneath the middle of the river. When you hear their footsteps above, split the frozen surface and send him and all his disciples plunging into the water. Then they can be taken in a single stroke.” The monster was delighted by these words and cried, “Excellent! Excellent!” He immediately left his watery palace, mounted the open sky, stirred up wind and snow, and brought a freezing cold that congealed the river into ice—but no more of that for now.

p.src: After master and disciples had admired the scene for a long while, they saw the elder of the Chen household order two young servants to sweep a path clear, while two others brought hot water for them to wash their faces. Presently they brought piping-hot tea and milk cakes, and carried in a brazier of charcoal as well. They all gathered in the side room and sat conversing with the master and his disciples. The Elder asked, “Good patron, do the seasons in your esteemed region distinguish spring, summer, autumn, and winter?” Old Chen laughed and said, “Though this is a remote place, only our customs and people differ from those of your great country. As for crops and livestock of every kind, we share the same heaven and sun. How could we not have the four seasons?” Tripitaka said, “If you do have four seasons, why is there already such heavy snow and such bitter cold?” Old Chen replied, “Although it is still the seventh month, yesterday we entered the White Dew solar term, which marks the season of the eighth month. Here, frost and snow commonly arrive in the eighth month every year.” Tripitaka said, “That is very different from my eastern land, where such weather does not come until the onset of winter.”

p.src: As they spoke, more young servants came to set the table and invite them to eat porridge. After they had finished the porridge, the snow fell even more heavily than in the morning, and before long it lay some two feet deep on level ground. Tripitaka grew anxious and shed tears. Old Chen said, “Rest easy, Reverend Sir. Do not be troubled by the depth of the snow. My household has several hundredweight of grain, enough to support you gentlemen for half a lifetime.” Tripitaka said, “Good patron, you do not understand this poor monk’s distress. In years past I received an imperial commission by the sovereign’s grace. His Majesty came in full state to escort me beyond the pass, and the Tang emperor personally raised a cup to bid me farewell, asking, ‘When will you return?’ Knowing nothing then of the perils of mountains and rivers, I answered without thought, ‘Three years will suffice to fetch the scriptures and return to our country.’ Seven or eight years have now passed since our parting, yet I have not even beheld the Buddha’s face, and I fear I shall exceed the imperial time limit. And I also dread the ferocity of demons and monsters. That is why I am anxious. Today good fortune has allowed us to lodge in your noble residence, and last night my foolish disciples rendered a small service in return. I had truly hoped to ask for a boat to take us across the river. But unexpectedly this great snow has fallen from heaven and hidden all the roads. I do not know when I shall complete my mission and return to my homeland.” Old Chen said, “Rest easy, Reverend Sir. You have already passed so many days on the road—what difference can these few more make? Wait until the sky clears and the ice melts. Even if I must exhaust my household and fortune, I shall certainly arrange to send you across the river.”

p.src: After admiring them for a long while, everyone sat down in the snow grotto. They told the neighboring elders about the scripture pilgrimage, and then drank the fragrant tea that was offered. Old Chen asked, “Reverend gentlemen, do you drink wine?” Tripitaka said, “This poor monk does not drink, but my young disciples will take a few cups of meatless wine.” Old Chen was delighted and immediately ordered, “Bring vegetarian fruits and dishes, and warm some wine to drive the cold from our honored guests.” The servants at once brought in a table and placed it around the brazier. The disciples and the two neighboring elders each drank several cups, after which the fire and utensils were cleared away.

p.src: Before they knew it, evening was drawing on, and they were invited back to the hall for the evening vegetarian meal. They heard people in the street saying, “What bitter cold! The River of Heaven has frozen over.” Hearing this, Tripitaka said, “Wukong, if the river is frozen, what are we to do?” Old Chen said, “As the cold has come so suddenly, I imagine only the shallows near the banks have frozen.” The passersby said, “All eight hundred li are frozen smooth as a mirror, and people are walking across at the crossing.” When Tripitaka heard that people were walking on it, he wanted to go and see. Old Chen said, “Do not be hasty, Reverend Sir. It is late today; go and see tomorrow.” They then took leave of the neighboring elders. After finishing the evening meal, they once again rested in the side room.

p.src: When dawn came the next day, Bajie rose and said, “It was even colder last night. The river must surely be frozen over.” Tripitaka faced the doorway, bowed to Heaven, and said, “Great gods who protect the Faith, ever since your disciple began journeying west, I have worshiped the Buddha with a sincere heart and endured the hardships of mountains and rivers without uttering a single complaint. Now that I have come here, Heaven has graciously aided me by freezing the river. For now, your disciple offers thanks with empty hands; when I return with the scriptures, I shall report this to the Tang emperor and repay you with the utmost devotion.” When he had finished worshiping, he told Wujing to carry the horse so that they could cross the river over the ice. p.src: Tripitaka and the party reached the riverside and reined in their horses to look. Sure enough, people were walking across at the crossing. Tripitaka asked, “Benefactor, where are those people going over the ice?” Old Chen replied, “On the far side of the river lies the Women’s Kingdom of Western Liang. Those people are all merchants. Goods worth a hundred cash on our side can fetch ten thousand there; and goods worth a hundred cash there can likewise fetch ten thousand here. The profits are great and the capital small, so people risk life and death to make the journey. In ordinary years, five or seven people share a boat, sometimes more than ten, and cross the broad waters. Now that they see the river frozen over, they are staking their lives on crossing it on foot.” Tripitaka said, “Of all things in the world, fame and profit weigh most heavily. Those men, for profit, cast aside death and forget their lives; while I, your disciple, obey the imperial decree and fulfill my loyalty, yet do so only for fame. How much difference is there between us?” He ordered, “Wukong, quickly return to our benefactor’s house, pack the luggage, and saddle and harness the horse. Let us take advantage of this sheet of ice and hasten westward.” The Pilgrim smilingly assented.

p.src: Monk Sha said, “Master, as the saying goes, ‘In a thousand days one consumes a thousand measures of rice.’ We have already imposed upon the Chen household, so let us stay a few more days until the sky clears and the ice thaws, then arrange a boat to cross. In haste, I fear something may go wrong.” Tripitaka said, “Wujing, how can you hold such a foolish opinion? If it were the first or second month, with each day warmer than the last, we could wait for the ice to thaw; but this is the eighth month, when each day is colder than the one before. How could we expect the ice to thaw soon? Would that not delay our journey by another half year?”

p.src: Bajie leaped down from his horse. “Stop your idle chatter and let old Pig test how thick the ice is.” The Pilgrim said, “Idiot, when you tested the water the night before last, you could throw in a stone; but now the river is covered by thick ice. How can you test it?” Bajie said, “Brother, you do not understand. Let me strike it once with my rake. If I break through, the ice is thin and we shall not dare cross; if I cannot break it, the ice is thick, so why should we not go?” Tripitaka said, “Exactly. That makes sense.” The idiot hitched up his robe, strode to the riverside, raised the rake in both hands, and struck with all his might. There was a thud; he left nine white marks, and the shock made his hands ache fiercely. The idiot laughed. “We can cross, we can cross! It is frozen solid all the way to the bottom.”

p.src: Hearing this, Tripitaka was overjoyed. He returned to the Chen home with the others and ordered them to prepare for departure. The two old men pleaded with them to remain but could not persuade them, so they prepared dried provisions and parched grain, and made flatbreads and steamed buns for their journey. The whole household kowtowed in reverence, then brought out a tray of small pieces of gold and silver. Kneeling before them, they said, “Through your great kindness our child’s life was saved. Please accept this humble token toward a meal on your journey.” Tripitaka waved his hands and shook his head, refusing it. “I am a monk who has left the world. What use have I for wealth? Even on the road, I would not dare take it out. It is proper that I live from day to day by begging for alms. The provisions are quite enough.” The two elders pleaded again and again, until the Pilgrim pinched up a tiny piece with his fingertips, weighing about four or five mace, and handed it to the Tang Monk. “Master, consider it a small offering. Do not wholly disappoint the two elders’ goodwill.”

p.src: They then took leave of one another and went straight onto the ice at the riverside. The horse’s hooves slipped, nearly throwing Tripitaka from the saddle. Monk Sha said, “Master, this is difficult going.” Bajie said, “Wait. Let me ask Master Chen for some rice straw.” The Pilgrim asked, “What use is rice straw?” Bajie replied, “What would you know about it? We must wrap the horse’s hooves in straw so they will not slip and make Master fall.” Old Chen, hearing this from the bank, hurriedly ordered someone to fetch a bundle of rice straw from the house, while asking the Tang Monk to come ashore and dismount. Bajie wrapped the horse’s feet in straw, and only then did they tread onto the ice and proceed.

p.src: After leaving Old Chen and traveling three or four li from the riverbank, Bajie handed the nine-ringed priest’s staff to the Tang Monk and said, “Master, hold this crosswise while you ride.” The Pilgrim said, “This idiot is being sly. You were carrying the staff. Why are you making Master hold it now?” Bajie said, “You have never crossed ice before, so you do not understand. Wherever a river freezes, there are bound to be holes in the ice. If he should step into one and fall through, then without something held crosswise he would plunge straight into the water, and the ice would cover him like a great pot lid. How could he bore his way back up? Only by bracing himself like this will he be safe.” The Pilgrim laughed inwardly. “So this idiot is an old hand at crossing ice.” They all did as he advised: the elder held the priest’s staff crosswise, the Pilgrim held his iron cudgel crosswise, Monk Sha held his demon-subduing treasure staff crosswise, and Bajie carried the luggage on his shoulder with his rake across his waist. Thus reassured, master and disciples advanced. They continued without pause until evening, when they ate some of their provisions. They dared not stop for long, but by the radiance of stars and moon, seeing the frozen surface gleaming and stretching white into the distance, they pressed steadily onward, truly without ever checking the horse’s pace. Master and disciples could not close their eyes, but traveled through the entire night. At daybreak they ate more provisions and continued westward.

p.src: As they traveled, there suddenly came a loud cracking sound beneath the ice, which nearly frightened the white horse into falling. Tripitaka cried in alarm, “Disciples! Why was there such a loud noise?” Bajie replied, “This river has frozen exceptionally solid. It was the ground ice cracking. Perhaps here in the middle it has frozen solid all the way to the bottom.” Hearing this, Tripitaka was both startled and delighted. He urged his horse forward and pressed on, of which no more need be said.

p.src: Now the fiend, after returning to his underwater palace, had gathered the other spirits beneath the ice. They had waited a long while. As soon as he heard the clatter of hooves, he worked his magic below, and with a sharp crack burst the ice apart. The Great Sage Sun hastily leaped into the air; but the white horse had already fallen into the water, and the other three all plunged through as well.

p.src: The fiend seized Tripitaka and led his host of spirits straight back to the underwater palace, where he shouted sternly, “Where is Sister Mandarin Fish?” The old mandarin-fish dame came to the gate and bowed, saying, “Great King, I would not dare claim such an honor.” The fiend said, “Why do you say that, worthy sister? ‘Once a word is spoken, even a team of four horses cannot overtake it.’ I promised that if I followed your plan and caught the Tang monk, I would swear brotherhood with you. Today your splendid scheme has indeed succeeded and the Tang monk has been caught; how could I now go back on my word?” He ordered, “Underlings, carry over a table and sharpen the knives. Cut open this monk’s belly and gouge out his heart; flay his skin and carve up his flesh. Meanwhile, strike up the music. My worthy sister and I shall eat him together and so prolong our years and attain everlasting life.” The mandarin-fish dame said, “Great King, let us not eat him yet, lest his disciples come looking for him and make trouble. Let us patiently wait two days. If those fellows do not come seeking him, we can cut him open then, seat Your Majesty in the place of honor, gather all our kin around, and entertain you with music, song, and dance while we serve him up for Your Majesty to enjoy at leisure. Would that not be better?” The monster took her advice, hid the Tang monk behind the palace, and confined him beneath a stone coffer six feet long. Of this we shall speak no more for now.

p.src: Meanwhile Bajie and Sha Monk recovered the baggage from the water and loaded it onto the white horse. Parting the waterway, they surged through the rolling waves and emerged with the current streaming off their backs. The Pilgrim saw them from midair and asked, “Where is Master?” Bajie replied, “Master’s surname was Chen, and now his name is ‘Sunk to the Bottom.’ There is nowhere to look for him now. Let us get ashore first and decide what to do.” Bajie, as it happened, was Marshal Tianpeng descended to the mortal world, and in former days he had commanded the eighty thousand sailors of the Celestial River; Sha Monk had come from the River of Flowing Sands; and the white horse was a dragon prince of the Western Sea. Thus all three knew the ways of water. The Great Sage guided them from the sky, and in a short while they returned to the eastern bank, where they dried and groomed the horse and wrung out and straightened their clothes. The Great Sage lowered his cloud, and together they went to Chen Family Village. Someone had already reported to the two old men, “Of the four reverend pilgrims seeking the scriptures, only three have returned.” The brothers hurried out to meet them and saw that their clothes were indeed still wet. They said, “Reverend sirs, we tried so hard to persuade you to remain, but you refused. It seems nothing short of this would make you stop. Why do we not see the reverend Tripitaka?” Bajie said, “He is no longer called Tripitaka. His new name is Chen Sunk-to-the-Bottom.” The two old men wept and cried, “Alas, poor man! Alas, poor man! We said we would wait until the snow melted, prepare a boat, and see you across, but you stubbornly refused, and now it has cost him his life.” The Pilgrim said, “Old man, do not grieve over someone who is as good as ancient history. I guarantee that my master is alive and well. I know for certain that the Great King of Numinous Power has used some magic trick to carry him off. Set your mind at ease. Have our clothes washed and our travel documents dried, and get fodder for the white horse. Once we brothers find that villain, rescue our master, and utterly destroy the monster root and branch, we shall rid your entire village of this lasting menace, so that you may live in peace forever.” When old Chen heard this, his heart filled with joy, and he at once ordered a vegetarian meal to be prepared.
